title: Applications of Ampere's Circuital Law
short_intro: Ampere's circuital law relates the line integral of the magnetic field B along a closed loop to the net algebraic current passing through the surface bounded by the loop. It serves as a powerful analytical tool for determining magnetic fields produced by highly symmetric current distributions.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Calculation of magnetic field due to a long straight current-carrying wire, infinite sheet of current, and inside a long straight solenoid using Ampere's circuital law.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Magnetic field calculations for a toroidal solenoid, thick cylindrical conductors, coaxial cables, and boundary conditions for magnetic fields.

prerequisites: Line integrals and closed path integration in vector calculus
Biot-Savart law and the principle of superposition
Concept of enclosed current and surface threading in magnetostatics

concept_notes.heading: Statement of Ampere's Circuital Law
bullets: The line integral of the magnetic field vector B around any closed loop is equal to μ<sub>0</sub> times the total steady current I<sub>enclosed</sub> threading the surface.
Mathematically expressed as ∮ B · dl = μ<sub>0</sub> I<sub>enclosed</sub>, where μ<sub>0</sub> is the permeability of free space.
It is valid for steady currents and holds universally in magnetostatics, analogous to Gauss's law in electrostatics.

concept_notes.heading: Symmetry Requirements for Application
bullets: The application of Ampere's law to evaluate B analytically requires high spatial symmetry (cylindrical, planar, or toroidal).
An Amperian loop must be chosen such that the magnitude of B is constant along the path and B is either parallel or perpendicular to the path element dl.
When B is perpendicular to dl, the dot product vanishes; when parallel and uniform, B factors out of the integral.

concept_notes.heading: Magnetic Field of a Long Straight Solenoid
bullets: An ideal solenoid is treated as closely wound helical turns where the magnetic field outside is zero and uniform inside along the axis.
An rectangular Amperian loop is chosen with one side parallel to the axis inside and the opposite side far outside where B = 0.
The field magnitude depends strictly on the turn density n and current I, independent of the radius of the solenoid.

concept_notes.heading: Magnetic Field of a Toroidal Solenoid
bullets: A toroid is a hollow circular ring clothed with closely spaced current-carrying turns, confining the magnetic field entirely within the core.
Due to axial symmetry, the Amperian loop is a circle of radius r concentric with the toroid axis.
The magnetic field drops to zero in the open space interior to the inner radius and exterior to the outer radius of the toroid.

derivations.title: Magnetic Field Due to an Infinite Straight Current-Carrying Wire
derivations.conditions: Steady current I in an infinitely long, thin straight wire, evaluated at a perpendicular distance r.
steps: Establish cylindrical symmetry where magnetic field lines form concentric circles around the wire.
Choose a circular Amperian loop of radius r centered on the wire, lying in a plane perpendicular to it.
Evaluate the line integral ∮ B · dl = B ∮ dl = B(2πr) since B is uniform in magnitude and parallel to dl everywhere on the loop.
Equate the line integral to μ<sub>0</sub>I<sub>enclosed</sub> according to Ampere's circuital law: B(2πr) = μ<sub>0</sub>I.

derivations.title: Magnetic Field Inside and Outside a Long Straight Solenoid
derivations.conditions: Solenoid of length L with N total turns, turn density n = N/L, carrying current I.
steps: Consider a rectangular Amperian loop of length h, with one side of length h inside the solenoid parallel to the axis, one side outside where B=0, and two radial sides perpendicular to the field lines.
Compute the line integral over the four segments: the integral vanishes along the two radial sides (B ⊥ dl) and the outside side (B = 0).
The total line integral reduces to the contribution along the inner side of length h: ∮ B · dl = Bh.
Calculate the enclosed current: the number of turns enclosed by the loop is nh, so I<sub>enclosed</sub> = nhI.

graphs_and_experiments.title: B versus r for a Long Straight Conductor
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot showing B on the y-axis and radial distance r on the x-axis. For r < R (inside), B increases linearly (B ∝ r). For r > R (outside), B drops off in a rectangular hyperbola (B ∝ 1/r).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates how magnetic field behavior transitions from interior current distribution to exterior field dependence.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in multiple-choice questions asking to identify correct graphical variations of B with distance for solid conductors.

graphs_and_experiments.title: B versus r for a Toroidal Solenoid
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot where B is zero for r < a (inner radius), follows a 1/r curve between a and b (core region), and drops abruptly to zero for r > b (outer radius).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Confines magnetic field strictly to the core volume, demonstrating the ideal shielding property of toroids.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently used to test understanding of non-zero regions of magnetic field in closed geometries.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Mapping Magnetic Field of a Solenoid using Iron Filings or Compass
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A schematic showing parallel field lines inside the solenoid looping around to form continuous closed paths outside.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that magnetic field lines are continuous closed loops with no magnetic monopoles.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions on directional properties and continuity of B-fields.

solved_numericals.question: A long straight wire carries a current of 10 A. Calculate the magnitude of the magnetic field at a perpendicular distance of 5 cm from the wire.
solution_steps: Identify given values: I = 10 A, r = 5 cm = 0.05 m, μ<sub>0</sub> = 4π × 10<sup>-7</sup> T m/A.
State the formula for a straight wire: B = (μ<sub>0</sub>I) / (2πr).

solved_numericals.question: A solenoid is 0.5 m long, has 500 turns of wire, and carries a current of 2 A. Find the magnitude of the magnetic field inside the solenoid near its center.
solution_steps: Calculate turn density n = N / L = 500 / 0.5 = 1000 turns/m.

solved_numericals.question: A toroidal solenoid with a mean radius of 0.2 m has 1000 turns wound uniformly. If it carries a current of 0.5 A, find the magnetic field at a point inside the core at distance 0.2 m from the center.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: N = 1000, r = 0.2 m, I = 0.5 A.
State formula for toroid field: B = (μ<sub>0</sub> N I) / (2πr).

assumptions_and_limitations: Ampere's circuital law in its standard integral form is strictly valid only for steady currents (magnetostatics) where electric fields do not change with time.
For time-varying electromagnetic fields, Maxwell's displacement current correction must be added to the right side of the law.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Ampere's circuital law can only be used to calculate magnetic fields when there is high symmetry.
common_misconceptions.correct: Ampere's law is always true for any closed loop and any current distribution, but it is only useful for calculating B analytically when high symmetry allows B to be factored out of the integral.
common_misconceptions.why: The law is a universal topological relation, but algebraic evaluation requires symmetry.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The enclosed current in Ampere's law includes currents situated outside the Amperian loop.
common_misconceptions.correct: Only currents that pierce through the open surface bounded by the Amperian loop contribute to I<sub>enclosed</sub>.
common_misconceptions.why: External currents produce magnetic fields that contribute to B at every point on the path, but their net circulation around the closed loop sums to zero.

quick_revision: Applicable only for steady currents unless Maxwell's displacement current is included.
